title: The Only Fever in the World
subtitle: Krishna spares the defeated Jvara and grants him dominion over fever
story:
An invisible voice spoke out of the sky, and the great battle of Sonitpura came to a halt.

The war between Krishna and the thousand-armed king Vana had drawn the gods themselves onto the field. Vana was Shiva's devoted servant, and Shiva had sent his own creatures to fight for him — among them Jvara, the fever. The burning sickness had slipped inside Krishna's own body the moment it was struck down: for a while Krishna's movements had slackened, his steps had grown heavy, his hair stood on end, and he had yawned and sighed without cease, supporting himself with one hand on the ground until, after a long time, the great yogi shook the weakness off. He had drawn the demon out by creating from his own energy a second Jvara — a fever more dreadful than the first, terrible to all creatures — which had seized the original by force and dragged it from his body. Now the creature lay pinned in Krishna's hands, and Krishna, angry, threw him down on the earth and was about to tear him into pieces.

Then the invisible voice spoke from the sky: "O Krishna, large-armed Krishna, enhancer of the delight of the Yadavas, do not kill this Jvara. He is worthy of being protected by you."

Krishna, the lord of the past, the present and the future, the great preceptor of the world, heard it and let the fever go.

Jvara rose and prostrated himself at Krishna's feet with bent head. "O descendant of Yadu, O Govinda, hear what I have to submit unto you. I pray for this one boon only: that I may be the only Jvara in this world, and no one else may flourish."

"It is proper to confer a boon on one who prays for it," Krishna said, "and you have sought my protection. Fare well, Jvara. You will have what you pray for. As before, you will be the only fever — and may the one I created dissolve in me."

And the counter-fever that Krishna had made melted back into his own being, as frost melts into the morning.

Then Krishna told the fever how it would range through the world from that day on. "Divide yourself into three parts: with one, possess the four-legged animals; with the second, the immobile objects; with the third, human beings. And with the fourth portion of your third part, you will always live among the birds." Among mankind the fever would come in four forms, returning every day, after two days, after three days, and after four days. In trees it would live as the insect and the blight that withers the leaves and turns them pale; in fruits, as the disease called Aturya; in lotuses, as frost; in the earth, as drought; in water, as the weed Neelika; in peacocks, as the growing of the crest; in mountains, as mineral; in cows, as the sickness called Khoraka. "With your very sight and touch," Krishna said, "animals will lose their lives. Only gods and men will be able to withstand you."

Jvara was delighted. With folded hands he saluted Krishna. "I am blessed, Madhava, that you give me sovereignty over all creatures and objects. I wish to carry out any other order of yours — order me what I am to do. I was created long ago by Hara, the slayer of Tripura. Now, vanquished by you in battle, I have become your servant. You are my master."

"Then hear the resolution I cherish," Krishna said. "Any man who salutes me and attentively reads this account of the prowess of my arms in the great battle will be freed from fever."

"So be it," Jvara said.

Having received his boon and given his promise, the fever saluted Krishna and left the battlefield — carrying with him, in the very shape of his existence, the mercy that had spared him.
reflection: Jvara asks not for safety but for supremacy — he wants to remain the only fever in the world — and Krishna grants the wish while redrawing its limits: the fever may range everywhere, but it returns in measured forms, and the telling of its defeat is promised to free men from it. Mercy, here, is not the erasure of an enemy but the reshaping of his power.
next_story_tease: But the fever was only one of Vana's defenders — Shiva himself was already riding toward the battlefield.
hero_scene: On the Sonitpura battlefield the defeated Jvara, a gaunt burning figure, prostrates with bent head at Krishna's feet while Krishna, radiant, raises a hand in blessing and the counter-fever he created dissolves into mist behind him.
